summary: Teach dividing a unit fraction by a whole number (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12) as the sharing/partition meaning of division: 'if one-third is shared among 4, how big is each part?' Splitting the shaded third into 4 pieces re-rules the whole bar into 3 × 4 = 12 equal parts, so each new piece is a twelfth — smaller than a third. Build the double-partition (3 then 4) visually on a bar or number line, verify with the inverse 1/12 × 4 = 1/3, and deliberately contrast with the sibling operation (whole ÷ unit fraction, e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5) so learners distinguish 'share it out — gets smaller' from 'how many fit — gets bigger', the commonest confusion in this pair.
misconceptions: Over-generalises the just-learned 'dividing by fractions makes bigger' and inverts: 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/3 × 4 = 4/3 (confuses partition with measurement division)
Gets 1/12 by a rule but cannot say why the pieces are twelfths — thinks they are still thirds
Treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers, dividing the wrong part (e.g. 1 ÷ 4 over 3)
Adds the whole number to the denominator: 1/3 ÷ 4 → 1/7

activities.title: Share a third four ways on a bar
steps: Start with a whole bar that has one-third shaded.
Apply a '÷4' cut to the shaded third so it splits into 4 equal parts.

Re-rule the WHOLE bar the same way: if your cuts run along the bar (crossing the third-lines), extend them across the whole bar; if they run across the bar like the third-lines, cut each of the other two thirds into 4 equal parts too. Count: the whole is now ruled into 12 equal parts.
Read off one little shaded piece and name it: it is one-twelfth, not a smaller third.
Say out loud where 12 comes from: 3 original parts, each cut into 4, gives 3 × 4 = 12.
Gather 4 of the twelfths back together to remake the original third, confirming 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.
Optionally repeat on a number line: split the 0–1/3 segment into 4 equal sub-segments and see each is 1/12 of the whole 0–1 line.
activities.insight: Sharing one-third among 4 cuts the whole into twelfths because the second cut (into 4) multiplies the first partition (into 3): 3 × 4 = 12. The answer is smaller than 1/3, and the denominator grows because the whole is re-partitioned more finely — this is the picture, not a memorised rule.

activities.title: Share vs. how-many-fit: the sibling contrast
steps: Work two questions side by side on bars: 'share 1/3 among 4' (1/3 ÷ 4) and 'how many fifths fit in 4?' (4 ÷ 1/5).
For each, say aloud which action is happening: splitting one piece into more pieces, or counting how many pieces fit.
Predict before computing whether each answer is bigger or smaller than the starting number, and why.
Match short stories ('share this third between four of you' / 'how many 1/5 cups fill 4 cups?') to the correct ÷ expression.

State the rule-of-thumb in meaning terms for these cases: sharing among 2 or more makes each part smaller than the amount shared; counting how many unit fractions (smaller than 1) fit into a whole number gives an answer larger than that whole number.
activities.insight: Dividing a unit fraction by a whole number (sharing) and dividing a whole number by a unit fraction (measuring how many fit) are different meanings with opposite size effects. Naming which is happening HERE prevents over-generalising 'dividing by fractions makes it bigger'.

activities.title: Build and solve your own sharing story
steps: Take a new case such as 1/6 ÷ 3 and write a short sharing story for it (e.g. 'share one-sixth of a pizza between 3').

Draw a bar with one-sixth shaded and split that sixth into 3 equal parts, then re-rule the whole the same way (extend cuts that cross the sixth-lines across the bar, or cut every other sixth into 3 too).
Count the total equal parts the whole is now cut into (6 × 3 = 18) and name one piece (1/18).
Verify with the inverse: 1/18 × 3 = 1/6.
Explain how you found the bottom number, referring to the two cuts, not an added-on rule.
activities.insight: The partition method generalises: for any unit fraction 1/n ÷ m, splitting each of the n parts into m re-rules the whole into n × m parts, so each piece is 1/(n×m). Whenever the fraction is shared among 2 or more (m ≥ 2) the piece is smaller than the original; sharing among 1 would leave it unchanged.

activities.title: Check understanding with targeted distractors
steps: Answer: 1/3 ÷ 4 = ? choosing from 1/12, 4/3, 1/7.
For the chosen answer, state in one sentence whether it is bigger or smaller than 1/3 and why.
On a blank bar, draw the split of a shaded third into quarters and re-rule the whole bar the same way (extend cuts that cross the third-lines, or cut each third into 4) to show the twelfths.
Answer the second-tier probe: 'Point to one small piece — how do you know it is a twelfth and not a smaller third?'
activities.insight: A secure answer is 1/12 WITH an explanation that the whole is cut more finely into twelfths; the characteristic errors are 4/3 (multiplying instead of dividing, possibly from over-applying 'dividing with fractions makes bigger') and 1/7 (adding the whole number to the denominator).

activities.title: Talk-through sharing (optional discussion scaffold)
steps: Take on a sharing-story role: 'split this third fairly between four of you'.
Discuss aloud whether each person's piece is bigger or smaller than a third, and justify it.
Explain how the pieces get their name (twelfths) by describing the cuts you would make.
activities.insight: Articulating the sharing structure and the size comparison in words reinforces the partition meaning and can surface rule-following when a learner cannot name why the pieces are twelfths.

checkQuestion: Work out 1/3 ÷ 4. Then explain why, using a picture or words — what is being shared or split, and is your answer bigger or smaller than 1/3?
checkAnswer: 1/12. Sharing one-third among 4 means splitting the third into 4 equal parts; cutting each third into 4 cuts the whole into 3 × 4 = 12, so each part is 1/12 — smaller than 1/3. Check: 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.
